question.text: A 5-year-old is brought into your office by his mother. His mother states that he is having 10-20 episodes per day where he stops responding to his mother and is found staring out of the window. During these periods, he blinks more frequently than normal, but returns to his normal self afterwards. These episodes last 30 to 60 seconds. His mother states that all of his milestones have been normal and he had an uncomplicated birth. His mother also denies any other recent illness. On exam, his vitals are normal. During one of these episodes in the office, his EEG shows three-per-second spike and wave discharge. What is the most likely diagnosis?

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The clinical presentation of brief (30-60 seconds), recurrent episodes of unresponsiveness with staring, frequent blinking, and a normal return to baseline, along with a three-per-second spike and wave discharge on EEG, strongly suggests absence seizures. The age of onset (5 years old) is also consistent with this diagnosis.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: The three-per-second spike and wave discharge on EEG is highly indicative of absence seizures.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Febrile seizures are typically associated with fever, which is denied in this case. Benign focal epilepsy is less likely given the generalized nature of the episodes and the absence of focal neurological signs. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy typically presents with myoclonic jerks, which are not mentioned. Hearing deficits can cause seizures, but the EEG findings are more specific to absence seizures.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The child's brief episodes of staring with blinking, rapid return to baseline, and EEG showing spike-and-wave discharges are classic features of absence seizures. These are generalized seizures with no post-ictal confusion, lasting 10-60 seconds, which aligns with typical absence seizure patterns. The absence of fever, normal milestones, and absence of other neurological abnormalities support a benign epilepsy with no structural cause.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: The EEG finding of three-per-second spike and wave discharge during an episode is the most specific indicator of absence seizures.
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Febrile seizures (A) were considered but ruled out due to no fever history. Benign focal epilepsy (B) is less likely as the seizures are generalized. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (C) typically presents with myoclonic jerks and usually occurs in older children. Hearing deficits (E) are not supported by the clinical presentation.

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The child presents with brief, frequent episodes of staring with blinking, lasting 30-60 seconds, occurring 10-20 times daily, with normal development and no fever or other triggers. The EEG shows 3-per-second spike-and-wave discharges, which is classic for absence seizures. This pattern is highly specific for absence epilepsy, especially in a child of this age.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: 3-per-second spike and wave discharge on EEG during an episode
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Febrile seizures are ruled out due to absence of fever; benign focal epilepsy typically involves motor symptoms, not staring; juvenile myoclonic epilepsy occurs in adolescence and involves myoclonic jerks; hearing deficits would not cause staring episodes or EEG abnormalities.

olmo3_7b.clinical_reasoning: The patient is a 5-year-old with daily brief, non-convulsive episodes characterized by staring and increased blinking, followed by full recovery. The EEG during an episode shows three-per-second spike and wave discharges, which is most consistent with absence epilepsy, especially given the age and the specific EEG finding. Other options like febrile seizure, benign focal epilepsy, and juvenile myoclonic epilepsy typically do not present with the described EEG pattern or daily brief, non-convulsive, reversible events.
olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: The EEG showing three-per-second spike and wave discharges during an episode is highly suggestive of absence seizures.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered: Febrile seizures (A) are usually associated with fever and are not typically seen daily without a temperature history. Benign focal epilepsy (B) presents with partial seizures and specific focal abnormalities on EEG, which are less likely here. Juvenile myoclonic epilepsy (C) has myoclonic jerks rather than staring and EEG changes. Hearing deficits (E) are unrelated to the seizure presentation and EEG findings.
